title: Neutral water and temperature
body: In pure water pH = pOH (a neutral solution), which gives pH = pOH = 7.0 only at 25°C, because Kw depends on temperature and neutral pH deviates from 7.0 at other temperatures.
ced_evidence: 8.1.A.3–8.1.A.4 The value of Kw is temperature dependent

title: Water autoionization constant, Kw
ced_evidence: 8.1.A.2 Water autoionizes with an equilibrium constant Kw

title: Strong base: [OH−] from group I vs group II hydroxides
body: A strong base dissociates completely, so [OH−] equals the initial concentration for a group I hydroxide and double the initial concentration for a group II hydroxide.
caution: Taking −log[OH−] gives pOH, not pH; convert to pH using pH + pOH = 14 at 25°C before reporting.
ced_evidence: 8.2.A.2 double the initial concentration of a group II hydroxide

title: Conjugate pair: Ka, Kb and Kw
body: K_w = K_a \times K_b, \qquad pK_w = pK_a + pK_b
ced_evidence: 8.3.A.6 For any conjugate acid-base pair … Kw = Ka × Kb

title: Weak base + strong acid: three cases
body: B(aq) + H3O+(aq) → HB+(aq) + H2O(l) goes quantitatively, and the pH depends on which species is left in excess.

items.label: Weak base in excess
items.meaning: A buffer forms; pH comes from the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation.

items.label: Strong acid in excess
items.meaning: pH comes from the moles of excess hydronium ion and the total volume of solution.

items.label: Equimolar
items.meaning: Slightly acidic; pH comes from the equilibrium HB+(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ B(aq) + H3O+(aq).

ced_evidence: 8.4.A.3 If the strong acid is in excess

title: Titration curve (pH vs. volume of titrant)
body: A plot of pH (y-axis) against volume of titrant added (x-axis) that summarizes titration results and is read for the equivalence and half-equivalence points.

items.label: Axes
items.meaning: pH against volume of titrant added.

items.label: Equivalence point
items.meaning: Moles of titrant equal moles of analyte originally present; used to find the analyte concentration; the pH here is set by the major species (neutral for strong–strong, basic for weak acid, acidic for weak base).

items.label: Half-equivalence point
items.meaning: For a weak acid or base, [HA] = [A−], so pH = pKa and pKa can be read from the curve.

items.label: Buffering region
items.meaning: Region of the weak acid or base titration where both members of the conjugate pair are present.

caution: Do not confuse the half-equivalence point (pH = pKa) with the equivalence point; the pH at the equivalence point is not the pKa.
ced_evidence: 8.5.A.1 A titration curve, plotting pH against the volume of titrant added

title: Polyprotic acid titration curves
body: A titration curve of a polyprotic acid can be read for the following information.

items.label: Major species
items.meaning: The major species present at any point along the curve can be identified.

items.label: pKa of each proton
items.meaning: The pKa associated with each proton of a weak polyprotic acid.

ced_evidence: 8.5.A.5 titration curves can be used to determine the number of acidic protons

title: Buffer solution
body: A buffer solution contains a large concentration of both members of a conjugate acid-base pair, so the conjugate acid reacts with added base and the conjugate base reacts with added acid, which stabilizes pH.
ced_evidence: 8.8.A.1 A buffer solution contains a large concentration of both members in a conjugate acid-base pair

title: Why small additions barely change buffer pH
body: Adding small amounts of acid or base does not significantly change the ratio [A−]/[HA], so the buffer's pH changes much less than it would without the buffer.
ced_evidence: 8.9.A.1 does not significantly change the ratio of [A−]/[HA]
